description: Medieval theft and violence, Tudor vagrancy laws, heresy, treason and the witch trials.
content_html:
Crime in Anglo-Saxon and Medieval England

The most common crimes in Anglo-Saxon and medieval England were those driven by poverty and opportunity: petty theft of food, livestock and tools, assault, and trespass. Petty theft was the bread-and-butter offence of the medieval courts. Alongside these everyday crimes sat a range of offences that reflected the particular character of medieval society: poaching the king’s deer was a serious crime not because of the value of the deer but because it violated the authority of the lord or king over his land. Crimes against property were, in practice, often crimes against social hierarchy.

Violence was widespread and culturally tolerated to a degree that would alarm us today. Men were expected to defend their honour with force; blood feuds between families could persist for generations. The law struggled to control private violence, partly because it lacked the enforcement tools to do so. Murder — defined as secret killing without witnesses — was treated more seriously than open homicide committed in public, because the secret killing deprived the community of the ability to respond collectively.

Key Fact

The most common medieval crimes were petty theft (food, livestock, tools) and assault. Poaching was treated harshly because it violated the power of landlords and the crown over forest and game — a political as well as criminal offence.

Anglo-Saxon Laws and Early Justice

Anglo-Saxon law recognised wergild — a payment system by which crimes were settled through compensation rather than punishment. The amount paid depended on the victim’s social rank: killing a nobleman cost far more than killing a peasant. This system placed a monetary value on human life, explicitly linking social hierarchy to legal worth. It also meant that wealthy families could effectively buy their way out of criminal liability, a pattern that would persist in various forms for centuries.

Vagrancy and the Tudor Poor Laws

The sixteenth century saw a new crime move to the centre of public anxiety: vagrancy. The dissolution of the monasteries (1536–1541) under Henry VIII removed a major source of poor relief. Population growth, rising food prices and the enclosure of common land drove thousands off the land and into the roads. Authorities feared these roaming, unemployed people as a source of disorder and potential rebellion. Tudor legislation responded harshly: the Vagabonds Act of 1531 authorised whipping for first-time vagrants; repeat offenders could be branded, mutilated or, eventually, executed.

Heresy was one of the most politically charged crimes of the sixteenth century. Under Henry VIII and Edward VI, Catholic practices became heretical; under Mary I (1553–1558), Protestant belief was the capital offence. Some 287 Protestants were burned at the stake under Mary, earning her the name “Bloody Mary” in Protestant tradition. The Marian persecution targeted ordinary people as much as prominent reformers, demonstrating that heresy prosecution could serve as a tool of political terror.

Treason was redefined dramatically under Henry VIII. The Treason Act of 1534 made it treasonous to deny the royal supremacy in words — not just in deeds. This allowed the crown to use treason charges against critics, intellectuals and even private citizens who questioned royal policy. Sir Thomas More was executed for treason in 1535 for refusing to swear the Oath of Supremacy. The broadening of treason law reflected the Tudor state’s anxiety about its own legitimacy.

Witch Trials in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries

The Witchcraft Act of 1563, passed under Elizabeth I, brought witchcraft under secular criminal law and imposed the death penalty where the victim died. It built on Henry VIII’s 1542 Act, which had first made witchcraft capital but was repealed in 1547; the 1563 Act did not make all witchcraft a capital offence. The new law reflected anxieties about popular superstition, religious instability and social disorder. Witch trials tended to target the poor and marginal, especially elderly women who had become social liabilities. Accusations often arose from local disputes, illness or misfortune — a neighbour’s cow dying after a quarrel could trigger a witch accusation.

The most intense witch panic in English history occurred in East Anglia during the 1640s, when Matthew Hopkins operated as self-styled Witchfinder General. Hopkins exploited the chaos of the English Civil War — the collapse of normal judicial oversight, social anxiety and religious extremism — to extract confessions through sleep deprivation and other coercive methods. Historians estimate that Hopkins was responsible for the execution of over 100 people, perhaps more, between 1644 and 1647. His activities were extraordinary even by the standards of the time and ended when sceptical judges began to challenge his methods.

Key Fact

The Witchcraft Act was passed in 1563. Matthew Hopkins operated as Witchfinder General in East Anglia during the 1640s, exploiting the disorder of the Civil War. He was responsible for the prosecution and execution of over 100 suspected witches, making his campaign the most deadly witch panic in English history.

The nature of crime did change between the medieval and early modern periods, but there were also important continuities. Petty theft remained the single most common offence throughout — the forms changed but the poverty that drove it did not. What genuinely changed was the addition of new categories of crime linked to political and religious upheaval: heresy, treason and witchcraft were largely products of the Reformation era. Vagrancy law also represented a new form of criminalisation — making poverty itself an offence — that had no direct medieval equivalent.
exam_tip_html: When answering a 4-mark ‘Describe Two Features’ question on medieval or Tudor crime, give a clear feature and then develop it with specific supporting detail: naming the Witchcraft Act (1563) or Matthew Hopkins, or explaining how heresy prosecutions changed under different Tudor monarchs, will earn the second mark per feature. Avoid vague generalisations such as “people were treated harshly.” For the 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ question, show how the nature of crimes changed from the medieval to the early modern era — adding new categories (heresy, treason, vagrancy) while retaining old ones (theft, assault).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Medieval crime was dominated by petty theft and assault; wergild allowed wealthy families to pay off criminal liability, embedding social hierarchy into the law.
  • The sixteenth century added new crimes: vagrancy (driven by enclosure, inflation and the dissolution of the monasteries), heresy and an expanded definition of treason under Henry VIII.
  • Witch trials peaked in the 1640s under Matthew Hopkins, whose campaign in East Anglia exploited Civil War disorder to prosecute over 100 people — the worst witch panic in English history.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of vagrancy as a crime in Tudor England.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. Students should note that vagrancy was the offence of wandering homeless without work or support, created by Tudor legislation responding to enclosure and population growth. The Vagabonds Act 1531 authorised whipping; repeat offenders faced branding or mutilation. Simple identification (1 mark); developed with legislation or consequence (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the witch trials in England during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: The Witchcraft Act of 1563, passed under Elizabeth I, transferred witchcraft from church courts to secular law and imposed the death penalty where the victim died — though not all witchcraft became a capital offence. Feature 2: Matthew Hopkins operated as Witchfinder General in East Anglia during the 1640s, using coercive methods to extract confessions and responsible for over 100 executions. Other valid features: trials targeted poor, elderly women; accusations arose from local disputes; Civil War chaos enabled persecution.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why heresy became such a serious crime in Tudor England.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: States heresy was a religious offence. Developing: Notes the Reformation changed which beliefs were criminal. Secure: Explains how the Reformation politicised religious belief — denying royal supremacy or practising the wrong faith became threats to state authority; uses the example of Mary I burning 287 Protestants. Mastering: Sustains analysis of how heresy law served as political control, linking the Treason Act of 1534 (making verbal denial of royal supremacy treasonous) to the broader pattern of the Tudor state using crime definitions to police loyalty and belief.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the wergild system in Anglo-Saxon England.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: Describes wergild as a payment for crimes. Developing: Explains that payments depended on the victim's rank. Secure: Analyses how wergild embedded social hierarchy into justice — a nobleman's life was valued more than a peasant's, and wealth could effectively buy immunity from criminal liability. Mastering: Evaluates significance at the time (it reduced blood feuds; it reflected a community-based rather than state-based justice system) and over time (it represented a continuity of wealth-based justice that persisted in various forms; its absence marks a genuine shift when the Norman state began to assert royal courts over local custom).

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree that the nature of crime changed significantly between the medieval era and the seventeenth century?
Give reasons for your answer. Refer to specific examples in your response.
practice_questions.marks: For change: heresy and treason became major new crimes after the Reformation; the Witchcraft Act 1563 criminalised a new category; vagrancy legislation made poverty itself criminal. Against (continuity): petty theft remained the most common offence throughout; assault and violence persisted; the underlying driver of poverty did not change. Emerging: Simple list of changes. Developing: Notes change and continuity without sustained argument. Secure: Argues a position, uses specific evidence from both eras. Mastering: Evaluates the degree of change, weighing new categories (politically-driven crime: heresy, treason, witchcraft) against continuity (poverty-driven petty crime), and reaches a justified conclusion about how significant the change was.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of treason as a crime in Tudor England.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks per feature. Feature 1: The Treason Act of 1534 dramatically expanded the definition to include verbal denial of royal supremacy, not just physical acts against the king. Feature 2: High-profile cases such as Sir Thomas More (executed 1535) showed that treason could be used against respected individuals who merely refused to swear loyalty to new religious settlements. Other valid features: execution was the standard punishment; treason charges could be politically motivated; it was used to silence opposition.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the wergild system in Anglo-Saxon England?
options: A form of trial by combat between accuser and accused
A system of compensation payments to the victim's family based on their social rank
A network of community watchmen who patrolled at night
A set of laws written by King Alfred the Great

knowledge_checks.q: Under which English monarch were 287 Protestants burned as heretics?
The _____ Act of 1531 authorised the whipping of first-time vagrants.
Matthew Hopkins operated as _____ in East Anglia during the 1640s, exploiting the disorder of the Civil War.
Match each crime to its correct description:
right: Holding religious beliefs contrary to official church doctrine
Wandering homeless without work or support
A compensation payment made to a victim's family

flashcard_questions.q: What was the most common crime in medieval England?
flashcard_questions.a: Petty theft, driven by poverty — stealing food, livestock or tools was the everyday offence that filled the medieval courts.
A system of compensation payments in Anglo-Saxon law, with amounts set by the victim's social rank.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was poaching treated so seriously in medieval England?
flashcard_questions.a: It violated the lord or king's authority over their land — a political as well as a criminal offence.

flashcard_questions.q: What triggered the wave of vagrancy in Tudor England?
flashcard_questions.a: Enclosure of land, population growth, rising prices and the dissolution of the monasteries (1536-1541).

flashcard_questions.q: What punishment did the Vagabonds Act of 1531 authorise for first-time vagrants?

flashcard_questions.a: Holding religious beliefs contrary to official church doctrine — a capital offence in Tudor England.

flashcard_questions.q: The Treason Act of 1534 expanded the definition of treason to include what?
flashcard_questions.a: Verbal denial of the royal supremacy — making words, not just actions, potentially treasonous.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was Sir Thomas More executed in 1535?
flashcard_questions.a: He refused to swear the Oath of Supremacy recognising Henry VIII as head of the Church.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Witchcraft Act of 1563 do?
flashcard_questions.a: Passed under Elizabeth I, it brought witchcraft under secular criminal law and imposed the death penalty where the victim died. It did not make all witchcraft a capital offence.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was Matthew Hopkins and when did he operate?
flashcard_questions.a: The self-styled Witchfinder General, active in East Anglia 1644-1647.

flashcard_questions.q: What conditions allowed Matthew Hopkins to prosecute so many people?
flashcard_questions.a: The chaos of the English Civil War collapsed normal judicial oversight and created intense social anxiety.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of crime is a continuity from the medieval era through to the early modern period?
flashcard_questions.a: Petty theft driven by poverty — it remained the most common offence throughout.

glossary_terms.definition: Minor theft or stealing of goods of low value, typically driven by poverty or opportunity.
A system of compensation payments in Anglo-Saxon law, by which a wrongdoer paid the victim or their family a sum determined by the nature of the offence and the victim's social rank.
The condition of wandering homeless without means of support, made a criminal offence by a series of Tudor statutes.
The holding of religious beliefs contrary to official church doctrine, treated as a crime against God and, under Tudor law, a capital offence.
The crime of betraying one's sovereign or state, under the Treason Act of 1351 including levying war against the king or adhering to his enemies.
Matthew Hopkins (c.1620-1647), who styled himself Witchfinder General and was responsible for the prosecution of more than 100 suspected witches in East Anglia between 1644 and 1647.

hero_image_caption: Tudor-era witch trial — witchcraft prosecutions peaked during the chaos of the 1640s Civil War.
